title: Interacting with AWS: Console, CLI, and SDKs

questions.prompt: What do the Console, CLI, and SDKs have in common?

options.text: They all make the same signed AWS service API calls, which IAM authorizes
They each use a completely different backend
Only the Console can create resources

questions.explanation: All three are front doors to the same AWS APIs. Requests are signed with credentials and then authorized by IAM regardless of which tool you use.

questions.prompt: You have a task you'll repeat several times a week. Which tool best fits?

options.text: The Console, clicking through each time
The AWS CLI, so it's scriptable and repeatable
Nothing — repeated tasks aren't possible on AWS

questions.explanation: The CLI is scriptable and repeatable, which suits recurring tasks. The Console is better for exploring and one-offs.

questions.prompt: The Python SDK for AWS is called ____.
questions.explanation: boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python; other languages have their own SDKs (JavaScript, Java, Go, .NET, and more).

questions.prompt: Match each tool to the situation it fits best.

pairs.right: Calling AWS from inside your application code

questions.explanation: Console for exploring, CLI for repeatable commands, SDKs for code, and IaC for consistent, version-controlled environments.

questions.prompt: Why should you never commit AWS access keys to a repository?

options.text: They are powerful, long-lived secrets — anyone with the repo gains access to the account

questions.explanation: Long-term keys are powerful secrets. Committing them exposes the account; keep them in ~/.aws/ or use temporary role/SSO credentials.

questions.prompt: Which command starts the one-time AWS CLI credential/setup process?
questions.explanation: `aws configure` prompts for an access key, secret key, default Region, and output format, storing them as a profile under ~/.aws/.
